intro.title: Understanding Molar Mass
intro.paragraph1: Molar mass is the mass of one mole (6.022 × 10²³ particles) of a substance, expressed in grams per mole (g/mol). For a compound, it's found by adding up the atomic mass of every atom in its formula — water, H₂O, has a molar mass of 2×(1.008) + 15.999 = 18.015 g/mol, because a water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. This calculator parses the formula you enter, counts every element (including inside parentheses or brackets, like the two hydroxide groups in Ca(OH)₂), and looks up each element's standard atomic weight to compute the total.
intro.paragraph2: The atomic weights this calculator uses are the IUPAC conventional standard atomic weights — essentially a weighted average of an element's naturally occurring isotopes, which is why they aren't whole numbers (chlorine's 35.45 reflects a natural mix of mostly chlorine-35 and some chlorine-37). A handful of the heaviest elements (technetium, promethium, and everything from polonium onward) have no stable isotopes and thus no natural mixture to average — for these, the value in brackets is the mass number of their most stable known isotope instead.
intro.paragraph3: Formulas with a middle dot, bullet, or period followed by a number represent hydrates — compounds that incorporate water molecules into their crystal structure, like CuSO₄·5H₂O (copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate). The number before the water tells you how many water molecules are bound per formula unit of the compound, and this calculator adds that water's mass on top of the anhydrous compound's mass to get the hydrate's total molar mass.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: Molar masses for a range of common compounds, computed by this calculator.

items.question: Why does capitalization matter when typing a formula?
items.answer: Each element symbol is exactly one uppercase letter, optionally followed by one or two lowercase letters — capitalization is how the parser tells elements apart from each other. "Co" is cobalt, but "CO" is two separate elements, carbon and oxygen, forming carbon monoxide; getting the case wrong changes which compound you're actually describing.

items.question: How does this calculator handle groups in parentheses or brackets?
items.answer: It reads everything inside the parentheses or brackets as its own sub-formula, then multiplies every element's count in that sub-formula by the number immediately following the closing bracket (or by 1 if no number follows). In Ca(OH)₂, that means the single oxygen and single hydrogen inside the parentheses each get counted twice, for a total of 2 oxygen and 2 hydrogen atoms.

items.question: What's the difference between molar mass and molecular weight?
items.answer: In practice, essentially nothing for most everyday purposes — both describe the same quantity (the mass of one mole of a substance), and both are typically reported in grams per mole. Chemists mostly use "molar mass" as the more general, formally correct term (it applies equally to ionic compounds and network solids, not just discrete molecules), while "molecular weight" is an older term technically specific to actual molecules.

items.question: Why do some atomic masses have brackets around them?
items.answer: A bracketed value, like technetium's [97], isn't a standard atomic weight at all — it's the mass number of that element's longest-lived known isotope. These elements have no stable isotopes, so there's no naturally occurring mixture of isotopes to average into a standard atomic weight the way there is for something like chlorine or carbon.

items.question: Can this calculator handle formulas with more than one hydrate dot?
items.answer: No — it supports a single hydrate separator (a middle dot, bullet, or period followed by a number), which covers the vast majority of real hydrate formulas like CuSO₄·5H₂O or MgSO₄·7H₂O. Formulas needing more than one such separator are extremely uncommon and outside this calculator's scope.

history.title: A Unit Named for a Word That Wasn't Even About Counting Yet
history.paragraph: The word "mole" entered chemistry in 1893, when German chemist Wilhelm Ostwald defined it in a laboratory manual as simply the mass in grams numerically equal to a substance's molecular weight — at that point a practical shorthand for weighing out chemicals, not yet tied to any specific count of particles. The now-famous number of particles in a mole traces back to Amedeo Avogadro's 1811 hypothesis that equal volumes of gas at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules, though Avogadro himself never calculated or named the number that would eventually bear his name.

modernDevelopments.title: From a Named Constant to a Defining One
modernDevelopments.paragraph: French physicist Jean Perrin coined the term "Avogadro's number" in 1908 to honor Avogadro, after Perrin's own experiments on Brownian motion provided the first reasonably precise measurement of that number — work that also helped settle the then-live scientific debate over whether atoms were physically real, and earned Perrin the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics. The relationship between the mole and Avogadro's number was inverted entirely in the 2019 revision of the International System of Units (SI): rather than measuring Avogadro's number from a physical mole defined by carbon-12, the mole is now defined by fixing Avogadro's number at exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³, permanently decoupling the unit from any physical artifact or isotope sample.

intro.title: Understanding Stoichiometry
intro.paragraph1: Stoichiometry is the calculation of how much of each substance participates in a chemical reaction, based on the balanced equation's coefficients. Those coefficients — the numbers in front of each formula, like the 2 in 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O — describe a fixed mole ratio: exactly 2 moles of H₂ react with exactly 1 mole of O₂ to produce exactly 2 moles of H₂O, no matter how large or small the actual reaction is. This calculator uses that ratio directly: moles of the target substance equal moles of the known substance multiplied by (target coefficient ÷ known coefficient).
intro.paragraph2: Because chemicals are measured by mass in a lab, not by counting individual molecules, converting to and from moles requires molar mass — the same calculation this site's Molar Mass Calculator performs. Given a known amount in grams, this calculator first divides by the known substance's molar mass to get moles; after applying the mole ratio, if the target amount is wanted in grams, it multiplies the target moles by the target substance's molar mass. Requesting moles on either side skips the corresponding conversion.
intro.paragraph3: This calculator assumes the equation you're working from is already balanced and that the reaction goes to completion with no leftover limiting reagent to account for — it performs the ratio-and-mass arithmetic once the coefficients are known, rather than balancing an unbalanced equation itself (a separate, more involved task that this site's Chemical Equation Balancer handles).

rows.calculation: 4 g of H2 (coefficient 2) → grams of H2O (coefficient 2)

items.question: Why do I need to enter the coefficients myself instead of the full equation?
items.answer: Parsing and correctly balancing an arbitrary chemical equation is a substantially harder problem than applying a ratio once the coefficients are already known — this calculator focuses specifically on the mole-ratio conversion step. If you don't have a balanced equation yet, this site's Chemical Equation Balancer can balance one for you first.

items.question: Does it matter which substance I call "known" and which I call "target"?
items.answer: No — the mole-ratio relationship works symmetrically. Whichever substance you have a measured amount of is the "known," and whichever one you want to find the amount of is the "target"; swapping them and re-entering the numbers the other way around gives you the reverse conversion.

items.question: Why does the calculator need molar mass at all if I'm just using mole ratios?
items.answer: Mole ratios convert moles to moles directly, but in practice you almost always start with (or want) a mass in grams, since that's what a lab balance measures. Molar mass is the conversion factor between grams and moles for each specific substance, so it's only needed at the entry and exit points of the calculation — not in the ratio step itself.

items.question: What happens if I mix up the coefficients from an unbalanced equation?
items.answer: The calculator will still compute a mathematically consistent answer, but it won't reflect real chemistry — the mole ratio has to come from a properly balanced equation to mean anything. Double-check that both sides of your equation have equal numbers of each type of atom before trusting the coefficients you enter.

items.question: Can this handle a reaction with more than two substances at once?
items.answer: Not directly in a single calculation — it converts between exactly one known and one target substance at a time. For a reaction with several products or reactants, run the calculator once per substance you want to find, always using the same known amount and its coefficient as the starting point.

history.title: A Word Coined for the "Art of Measuring" Chemical Elements
history.paragraph: German chemist Jeremias Benjamin Richter coined the term "stoichiometry" in his three-volume 1792–1793 work Anfangsgründe der Stöchyometrie oder Meßkunst chymischer Elemente ("Elements of Stoichiometry, or the Art of Measuring Chemical Elements"). Richter was convinced that chemical reactions followed strict mathematical laws, and his careful measurements of the weights of acids and bases needed to exactly neutralize each other led him to what's now called the law of reciprocal proportions — an early, quantitative precursor to the mole-ratio calculations this calculator performs, worked out decades before atoms or molecules were reliably countable.

modernDevelopments.title: The Reaction That Feeds Roughly Half the World
modernDevelopments.paragraph: The reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ used in this page's worked examples is the Haber-Bosch process, developed by Fritz Haber (lab-scale synthesis, 1909) and industrialized by Carl Bosch (1913) — work that earned each of them a separate Nobel Prize (Haber in 1918, Bosch in 1931). By fixing atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia for synthetic fertilizer at industrial scale, the exact 1:3:2 mole ratio in that single stoichiometric equation is credited with sustaining roughly half of current global food production, since most of the nitrogen in a typical human body today traces back through the food supply to ammonia made this way.

intro.title: Understanding Percentages
intro.paragraph1: A percentage expresses a number as a fraction of 100 — the word itself comes from the Latin per centum, "by the hundred." Writing a value as a percentage makes it easy to compare quantities of very different sizes on the same scale: whether a class has 20 or 200 students, saying 15% failed a test conveys the same relative information either way.
intro.paragraph2: This tool covers five distinct percentage calculations that are frequently confused with one another: finding a percentage of a number, finding what percentage one number is of another, percentage change (a directional comparison that uses the original value as its base), reverse percentage (working backward from a known result to the original number), and percentage difference (a symmetric comparison that does not treat either value as the "original").

diagram.caption: 27 of these 100 squares are shaded — this is literally what "27%" means: 27 parts for every 100.

intro.paragraph3: The distinction between percentage change and percentage difference trips up even experienced analysts. Going from 80 to 100 is a percentage change of +25%, using 80 (the original value) as the base. But the percentage difference between the same two numbers, which uses their average of 90 as the base instead, is about 22.2% — the same two numbers, two different questions, two different valid answers.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: Five worked examples, one for each calculation mode, showing the exact inputs and results.

items.question: What's the difference between percentage change and percentage difference?
items.answer: Percentage change is directional and always measures against the original value as its base — going from 80 to 100 is a +25% change, but going from 100 back down to 80 is a −20% change, even though it's the same two numbers. Percentage difference is symmetric: it measures the gap between two values against their average instead, so the percentage difference between 80 and 100 is about 22.2%, not 25%, because it divides by their average (90) rather than by the original value (80).

items.question: Why doesn't increasing a number by 20% and then decreasing it by 20% bring it back to where it started?
items.answer: Because each percentage is calculated from a different base. Increasing 100 by 20% gives 120. Decreasing that new number, 120, by 20% removes 24 (20% of 120), not 20, leaving 96 — not the original 100. The second percentage is always taken from whatever the first calculation produced, not from the original number.

items.question: What's the difference between a percentage point and a percent?
items.answer: If an interest rate rises from 5% to 7%, that is a rise of 2 percentage points — a simple subtraction — but it is also a 40% relative increase in the rate itself (2 is 40% of 5). Both statements are correct; they just answer different questions, and mixing them up is one of the most common errors in financial and political reporting.

items.question: How do I reverse a percentage calculation by hand?
items.answer: Divide the known result by the percentage expressed as a decimal. If 12 is 30% of an unknown number, divide 12 by 0.30 to get 40 — the same calculation this tool's "Reverse" mode performs automatically.

items.question: Why can't the "what percent" or "reverse" modes accept a zero base or zero percentage?
items.answer: Both calculations require dividing by that value, and division by zero is mathematically undefined. Rather than showing a meaningless result, the tool flags these cases directly.

items.question: Where do percentages show up in everyday financial decisions?
items.answer: Interest rates, inflation figures, sales tax, discounts, and investment returns are all expressed as percentages, because doing so lets amounts of very different sizes be compared on the same relative scale rather than as raw, hard-to-compare numbers.

history.title: From "Per Cento" to the Modern % Symbol
history.paragraph: Percentages were used in the commercial arithmetic of medieval Italy's trading cities well before they had a dedicated symbol. Interest, profit shares, and taxes were routinely calculated "per cento" — Italian for "per hundred" — and merchant manuscripts from the 15th century already abbreviate the phrase; a manuscript from around 1425 shows the abbreviation "pc" with a small circle standing in for the Italian ordinal ending, an early ancestor of the modern sign. Over the following two centuries the abbreviation was gradually simplified: by around 1650 it had taken a horizontal fraction-bar form, and by the 19th century the two circles had settled on either side of a diagonal stroke, giving the % symbol still used today.

modernDevelopments.title: Percentages in the Spreadsheet and Data Age
modernDevelopments.paragraph: The arrival of the electronic spreadsheet — starting with VisiCalc in 1979 and followed by Lotus 1-2-3 and Microsoft Excel — turned percentage-based financial modeling from a manual, error-prone exercise into something anyone could recompute instantly by changing a single cell. Percentages remain the default unit for describing change in economics, public health, and data journalism today, precisely because they let readers compare figures of very different scale — a country's GDP growth or a survey's approval rating — on the same intuitive footing.

intro.title: How Tipping Math Works
intro.paragraph1: A tip is calculated as a percentage of the bill, then optionally split evenly across everyone at the table. Because it scales with the bill rather than with the amount of work a server actually did, a percentage tip on an expensive bottle of wine adds far more than the same percentage on a modest plate of food — one reason some diners tip a flat amount on certain high-priced items regardless of the percentage they use for the rest of the check.
intro.paragraph2: Splitting a tip evenly rarely divides into a clean number, which is where rounding comes in. This tool's "round up" option takes each diner's raw share, rounds it up to the next whole currency unit, and folds the small difference into the tip rather than making anyone dig for exact change — a common real-world convenience that changes how the total is distributed, not the tip rate you actually asked for.

items.question: Should I tip on the pre-tax or post-tax bill amount?
items.answer: Most etiquette guides recommend tipping on the pre-tax subtotal, but tipping on the post-tax total is common practice and not considered rude — the difference between the two is usually small.

items.question: What's the difference between a tip and a service charge?
items.answer: A tip is voluntary and discretionary. A service charge — often added automatically for large groups — is typically mandatory and added to the bill by the establishment itself, and it doesn't always go entirely to the staff who served you. Check the receipt to see whether one is already included before adding an additional tip.

items.question: Is tipping mandatory?
items.answer: In most countries, no — it's a voluntary, discretionary sum. In the United States it's such a deeply embedded norm that skipping it for merely below-average (rather than genuinely bad) service is generally considered a breach of etiquette, unlike in many other countries where it isn't expected at all.

items.question: Why do restaurants add an automatic gratuity for large groups?
items.answer: It guarantees fair compensation for serving a large, often multi-course table, and prevents a tip from being silently split too thin across many diners who each assume someone else covered it adequately.

items.question: How does the round-up option change what I actually pay?
items.answer: It doesn't change the tip percentage you asked for — it rounds each diner's share up to the next whole currency unit so nobody needs exact change, with the small difference folded into the tip rather than kept as change.

items.question: How much should I tip for services besides restaurants, like haircuts or delivery?
items.answer: Common general norms in tipping-culture countries: 15–20% for hairdressers and barbers, 10–20% or a flat amount for food delivery depending on distance and conditions, and a few dollars per night for hotel housekeeping — though these vary by country. This tool is built around splitting a restaurant-style bill.

history.title: From European Aristocracy to the American Restaurant
history.paragraph: The word "tip" is not an acronym for "To Insure Promptness" — that's a persistent modern myth. Tipping's actual roots trace to master-servant customs in aristocratic Europe, where a servant could be rewarded with extra money for exceptional service beyond their wages. Wealthy Americans encountered the custom on European travels in the 1850s and 1860s and brought it home to appear sophisticated, but most Americans at the time viewed tipping as condescending and fundamentally undemocratic. It became widespread only after the Civil War, when it spread rapidly through service industries — including railroad companies that hired newly freed Black workers as porters at little or no base wage, expecting tips to make up their income. Several U.S. states, citing exactly this exploitative dynamic, banned tipping outright between roughly 1909 and 1926, though every one of those bans was eventually repealed.

modernDevelopments.title: From Cash on the Table to the Tip Screen
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Card-payment tip prompts and point-of-sale tip screens have extended tipping into venues that never took cash tips before, like coffee counters and self-checkout kiosks — a trend widely discussed under labels like "tip creep" and "tipping fatigue." At the same time, a smaller counter-movement of restaurants has experimented with no-tipping, service-included pricing instead, partly inspired by the model common across Western Europe. Regardless of how a tip is prompted, the underlying arithmetic — a percentage of the bill, split however many ways — is the same calculation this tool automates.

stackingReference.intro: Two discounts applied one after another never simply add up — here's the actual combined effect for common pairs.

intro.title: How Stacked Discounts Actually Work
intro.paragraph1: A discount is a percentage taken off a price, but when two or more discounts apply to the same item, they don't simply add together. Each successive discount applies to the already-reduced price, not the original one — so a $100 item that gets 30% off first drops to $70, and a further 10% off applies to that $70, not the original $100, bringing it to $63. The combined effect is 37% off, not the 40% you'd get by just adding the two rates.
intro.paragraph2: The same relationship runs in reverse. If you know a sale price and the discount rate printed on the tag, you can recover the original price by dividing the sale price by one minus the discount rate as a decimal — a $70 sale price at 30% off implies an original price of $70 ÷ 0.70 = $100. This is useful for verifying a retailer's claimed "original price," or simply for figuring out what something cost before a markdown you know the rate of.

diagram.caption: Each discount applies to the already-discounted price, not the original — so two discounts stack to less than their sum: 30% + 10% is 37% off in total, not 40%.

items.question: Why isn't 30% off plus 10% off the same as 40% off?
items.answer: Because the second discount applies to the price after the first one, not to the original price. $100 at 30% off is $70; a further 10% off applies to that $70, removing $7, not $10 — for a combined $63 final price, which is 37% off the original, not 40%.

items.question: Does the order of stacked discounts change the final price?
items.answer: No — multiplying percentages together is commutative, so 30% off then 10% off produces exactly the same final price as 10% off then 30% off. A retailer might still restrict the order for business reasons, like excluding an already-clearance item from an additional coupon, but the arithmetic itself doesn't care about order.

items.question: How do I find the original price if I only know the sale price and the discount rate?
items.answer: Divide the sale price by one minus the discount rate expressed as a decimal. A $70 item marked 30% off had an original price of $70 ÷ 0.70 = $100. This tool's "Find Original Price" mode performs exactly this calculation.

items.question: What's the difference between a discount and a markdown?
items.answer: The terms are often used interchangeably, but retailers typically distinguish them: a discount is usually a temporary, promotion- or coupon-driven price cut, while a markdown is usually a longer-term reduction to the standing shelf price meant to clear inventory.

items.question: Why do some stores advertise a discount in dollars and others in percent?
items.answer: Research on discount framing has found that a percentage-off discount tends to look more generous on a lower-priced item, while a dollar-off discount tends to look more generous on a higher-priced item — so retailers often choose whichever framing makes an identical price cut appear larger for that item's price tier.

items.question: Does a bigger percentage discount always mean bigger savings in dollar terms?
items.answer: No. A 50% discount on a $20 item saves $10, while a 10% discount on a $300 item saves $30 — the percentage rate alone doesn't tell you the actual amount saved, which is exactly why this tool always shows both figures side by side.

history.title: How the Fixed Price Tag Made "Percent Off" Possible
history.paragraph: Before the mid-19th century, most retail prices in the United States were individually negotiated through haggling, so there was no single stable reference point for a discount to apply against — a "good deal" was whatever price a particular haggling session produced. That changed with Philadelphia merchant John Wanamaker, who introduced marked, fixed price tags at his Oak Hall clothing store in 1861 and formalized a strict "one price" policy across his stores by 1871, paired with one of the first money-back guarantees in American retail. A fixed, marked price is exactly what makes a later "25% off" sale tag a specific, verifiable claim rather than just another opening bid to haggle down from — the arithmetic this tool automates only means something once there's a stable original price to calculate it against.

modernDevelopments.title: From the Clearance Rack to Black Friday
modernDevelopments.paragraph: The term "Black Friday" didn't start as a retail slogan — Philadelphia police coined it in the 1950s and 60s as a complaint about the traffic jams and unruly crowds that swamped the city the day after Thanksgiving, and local merchants unsuccessfully tried to rebrand it as the friendlier "Big Friday." It wasn't until the term spread nationally in the 1980s that retailers reframed it around the idea of stores finally turning a profit — going "into the black" — for the year. Today's version of the same clearance-sale logic runs largely on software: personalized coupon codes, algorithmically timed flash sales, and abandoned-cart discount emails all apply the identical stacked-percentage math this tool calculates, just triggered automatically instead of printed on a tag.

ratesReference.title: US Sales Tax Snapshot
ratesReference.intro: Unlike VAT elsewhere, US sales tax isn't one national rate — states set a base rate, and counties, cities, and districts stack more on top. A few reference points:
ratesReference.source: Source: Tax Foundation, State and Local Sales Tax Rates, Midyear 2026 (as of July 1, 2026). Figures are population-weighted average combined state + local rates; your actual local rate may differ.

intro.title: How Sales Tax Actually Works
intro.paragraph1: Sales tax is a percentage of a purchase's price added at the register and collected by the seller, who remits it to state and local governments. Unlike a value-added tax (VAT), which many countries outside the US charge in smaller increments at every stage of production and only on the value newly added at each step, US-style sales tax is collected exactly once, at the final retail sale to the end consumer — a $100 item taxed at 8% simply costs $108 at checkout.
intro.paragraph2: The catch is that "8%" in the US is almost never set in one place. A state government sets a base rate, and counties, cities, and special taxing districts can each layer their own smaller rate on top, all added together into one combined rate charged at the register — which is why identical purchases a few miles apart can carry different tax amounts. The relationship also runs in reverse: if a receipt shows only the tax-inclusive total, dividing it by one plus the combined rate as a decimal recovers the pre-tax price — a $108 total at a known 8% rate implies a $108 ÷ 1.08 = $100 pre-tax price, useful for expense reports or accounting where the pre-tax amount is what matters.

diagram.caption: Sales tax grows a subtotal into a total — the reverse of a discount, which shrinks a price. $100 subtotal + 8% tax ($8) = $108 total.

items.question: Is sales tax the same rate everywhere?
items.answer: No. Unlike a national VAT, US sales tax is set state by state, and most states let counties, cities, and special districts add their own rate on top — so the combined rate charged at the register can vary block by block, not just state by state.

items.question: How is sales tax different from VAT?
items.answer: Sales tax is collected once, at the final retail sale to the end consumer. VAT, used by most countries outside the US, is collected in smaller amounts at every stage of production, with businesses claiming credit for VAT they already paid on their own inputs — the two can produce a similar final price but get there through very different mechanics.

items.question: Why did two receipts for the same $100 purchase show different tax amounts?
items.answer: Almost certainly a different combined local rate — the state base rate plus whatever county, city, and district rates apply at each specific location, which can differ even between two stores a short drive apart.

items.question: How do I find the pre-tax price from a receipt that only shows the total?
items.answer: Divide the tax-inclusive total by one plus the tax rate expressed as a decimal. A $108 total at 8% tax implies a pre-tax price of $108 ÷ 1.08 = $100. This tool's "Extract From Total" mode performs exactly this calculation.

items.question: Do all US states charge sales tax?
items.answer: No — Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, and Oregon charge no statewide sales tax at all. Alaska charges no state-level tax either, but unlike the other three, it allows individual municipalities to levy their own local sales tax.

items.question: Do online purchases charge sales tax?
items.answer: Almost always now, even from out-of-state sellers. Following the Supreme Court's 2018 Wayfair decision, states can require a retailer to collect sales tax once it crosses a sales or transaction threshold in that state, regardless of whether it has any physical presence there — which is why most online checkouts now calculate a locally correct tax automatically.

history.title: Mississippi's Depression-Era Invention
history.paragraph: The first broad-based state sales tax in the US is less than a century old. Facing collapsed property tax revenue as the Great Depression gutted its overwhelmingly agricultural economy, Mississippi enacted a 2% general sales tax in 1930 — the first state to tax retail sales broadly as a general revenue source, rather than as a narrow excise on a handful of specific goods. The idea spread fast: within the following decade, roughly two dozen more states adopted their own version of the same mechanism, and today 45 states plus Washington, D.C. levy one.

modernDevelopments.title: From Storefronts to Server Farms
modernDevelopments.paragraph: For decades, a state could only require a business to collect its sales tax if that business had a physical presence there — a rule the Supreme Court set in 1967 and reaffirmed in 1992's Quill Corp. v. North Dakota, which let early catalog and online retailers ship into a state tax-free as long as they had no local store or warehouse. That changed in 2018, when South Dakota v. Wayfair, Inc. overturned the physical-presence rule and replaced it with "economic nexus" — a seller can now owe sales tax in a state purely by crossing a threshold of sales or transactions there, regardless of whether it has ever set foot in it. Within a few years, nearly every state with a sales tax adopted its own economic-nexus threshold, which is the reason almost every online checkout today calculates a locally correct tax amount automatically.

intro.title: How Image Compression Actually Works
intro.paragraph1: Every image format makes the same fundamental choice: lossless, which shrinks a file while preserving every original pixel exactly (PNG), or lossy, which discards some visual detail permanently in exchange for dramatically smaller files (JPEG, and WebP in its default mode). Lossless compression works like a more efficient way of writing down the same information — nothing is thrown away, so decompressing always reconstructs the exact original bytes. Lossy compression instead identifies the detail human eyes are least likely to notice — subtle color gradients, fine texture — and discards it outright, which is why the same JPEG saved and reopened repeatedly slowly degrades: each pass discards a little more.
intro.paragraph2: JPEG's specific technique is the discrete cosine transform (DCT): it splits an image into small blocks and represents each one as a sum of smooth wave patterns, then keeps only the low-frequency waves that matter most to human perception — a typical JPEG at default quality discards roughly 90% of the raw pixel data this way, and still looks essentially unchanged to most viewers. This tool converts entirely inside your browser via the Canvas API, so no image ever leaves your device.

diagram.caption: Lossless compression can always reconstruct the exact original; lossy compression permanently discards detail to shrink the file further.

items.question: Which format should I actually use?
items.answer: PNG for screenshots, logos, or anything needing transparency or perfectly sharp edges. JPEG for photos where you want maximum compatibility. WebP for photos on the web generally — it usually beats JPEG at the same visual quality and virtually all current browsers support it.

items.question: Does converting PNG to JPEG and back to PNG lose quality twice?
items.answer: Yes, and this is a genuinely common mistake. Once an image passes through a lossy format like JPEG, the detail that format discarded is gone permanently — converting the result back to PNG just locks in that already-degraded version losslessly. Repeatedly re-saving as JPEG compounds the loss further each time. Always keep (or start from) the highest-quality original you have.

items.question: What does the "quality" slider actually control?
items.answer: For JPEG and WebP, it controls how aggressively the encoder discards fine visual detail — lower quality means smaller files but more visible artifacts, especially blockiness around sharp edges and color banding in smooth gradients. It has no effect for PNG, since PNG is lossless and doesn't have a quality/detail tradeoff to make.

items.question: Why does resizing an image before converting help so much?
items.answer: File size for a lossy format scales roughly with pixel count, so halving both width and height cuts the pixel count — and therefore roughly the file size — to about a quarter. Resizing to the dimensions you'll actually display an image at is usually a bigger size win than tightening the quality slider on an oversized image.

items.question: Is WebP support universal now?
items.answer: Essentially yes for viewing — every major browser (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge) has supported displaying WebP images since 2020 or earlier. The one place it can still cause friction is older software (some older design tools, some email clients) that can't open a .webp file directly, which is worth checking before using it somewhere JPEG or PNG would be safer.

items.question: Is my image uploaded anywhere when I use this tool?
items.answer: No — every step, including reading the file, resizing, and re-encoding it into a new format, happens locally in your browser using the Canvas API. The image is never transmitted anywhere.

history.title: A Six-Year Committee Question: How Much Can an Eye Forgive?
history.paragraph: The Joint Photographic Experts Group formed in 1986 as a joint effort between two international standards bodies, tasked with a question that had no clean engineering answer: how much of a photograph's raw data could be discarded before a human eye would notice? After six years evaluating candidate compression methods, the committee published what the world now calls JPEG in September 1992, built around the discrete cosine transform — a technique first proposed for image compression back in 1972. The result, still in near-universal use today, routinely throws away roughly 90% of a photo's raw pixel data while looking, to most eyes, essentially unchanged.

modernDevelopments.title: From a Patent Dispute to a Video Codec's Side Project
modernDevelopments.paragraph: PNG's origin traces to a legal fight, not a technical one: when Unisys announced in December 1994 that it would start charging licensing fees for the LZW compression method used inside the hugely popular GIF format, engineers - some of whom had worked on JPEG - moved quickly to design a free, open replacement, releasing the first PNG specification in 1996 with real transparency and no patent encumbrance. WebP arrived by a completely different route in 2010: after acquiring video codec company On2 Technologies, Google adapted the intra-frame compression technology built for its VP8 video codec — the part that compresses a single video frame on its own — into a standalone still-image format, reporting roughly 39% smaller files than equivalent-quality JPEGs in real-world testing.

intro.title: How JSON Actually Works
intro.paragraph1: JSON only has two structural types — objects (key-value pairs in '{ }') and arrays (ordered lists in [ ]) — and four primitive types inside them: strings, numbers, booleans, and null. That's the entire grammar. There's no date type, no comments, no trailing commas, and no unquoted keys, and every one of those "missing" features is a deliberate simplicity choice, not an oversight — it's exactly what makes JSON trivial to parse correctly in any language, unlike formats with more flexible, ambiguous grammars.
intro.paragraph2: That same strict grammar is also why a single missing comma or quote makes an entire JSON document fail to parse, with no partial recovery — which is exactly the problem this tool's error reporting solves. Rather than surfacing whatever cryptic message your browser's JavaScript engine happens to produce (these vary by engine and aren't always reliable), this tool runs its own dedicated JSON grammar check to point at the exact line and column of the first syntax deviation.

diagram.caption: Every JSON value is exactly one of six types — two structural (object, array) and four primitive (string, number, boolean, null). There is nothing else in the grammar.

examples.intro: Four examples showing exactly how formatting settings change the output for the same input.

items.question: Why does my JSON fail to parse even though it looks correct?
items.answer: Almost always one of a handful of invisible-looking mistakes: a trailing comma before a closing } or ], an unquoted or single-quoted key, a stray comment (JSON has no comment syntax at all), or a number with a leading zero. This tool's error message points at the exact line and column of the first one it finds.

items.question: What's the difference between JSON and a JavaScript object literal?
items.answer: JSON is a strict subset of JavaScript object-literal syntax: JSON requires double-quoted keys and strings, allows no trailing commas, no comments, no functions, and no undefined — a JavaScript object literal allows all of those. Every valid JSON document is a valid JS object literal, but not the other way around.

items.question: Why sort object keys — doesn't order not matter in JSON?
items.answer: Order genuinely doesn't affect meaning to a JSON parser, but it matters enormously for humans and for tools: sorting keys makes two versions of similar data diff cleanly in version control or a code review, instead of showing every line as changed just because key order shifted.

items.question: Is my JSON data sent to a server when I use this tool?
items.answer: No — formatting, validation, and minifying all run entirely in your browser. Nothing you paste here is transmitted anywhere, which matters if the JSON contains real data like API responses or configuration with sensitive values.

items.question: What's the difference between minifying and formatting?
items.answer: Formatting adds indentation and line breaks to make JSON readable for humans; minifying strips every unnecessary whitespace character to make the file as small as possible for network transfer. Both represent identical data — a JSON parser treats them exactly the same.

items.question: Why do some JSON files use 2-space indentation and others 4?
items.answer: There's no technical difference — indentation is purely cosmetic and ignored by every parser. 2 spaces is the more common convention in JavaScript/web ecosystems (keeping deeply nested structures narrower), while 4 spaces is more common in Python-influenced style guides; some codebases use tabs specifically so each developer's editor can render the width they prefer.

history.title: How a Trading Card Game Simplified the Web
history.paragraph: JSON wasn't designed in a standards committee — it was discovered, in Douglas Crockford's own words, not invented. While building a browser-based virtual trading card game called Cartoon Orbit at State Software in 2001, Crockford grew frustrated with how heavy XML was for constantly syncing small pieces of state between a low-powered client and the server. He noticed that JavaScript's own object-literal syntax — the '{key: value}' notation already built into the language — was already a lightweight, human-readable way to represent structured data, so he named it, wrote a formal grammar for it, and registered json.org in 2002. He deliberately designed the specification to be usable from any programming language, not just JavaScript, which is exactly why it spread so far beyond its browser origins.

modernDevelopments.title: From API Responses to a Native Database Type
modernDevelopments.paragraph: JSON's first standardization arrived as RFC 4627 in 2006, later replaced by RFC 7159 and finally today's RFC 8259 in 2017, each revision tightening ambiguities the earlier specs had left open. Its adoption accelerated as REST APIs displaced the far heavier XML-based SOAP standard through the 2000s and 2010s. The more recent shift is JSON moving beyond being just a network format: PostgreSQL added a dedicated binary JSON column type (JSONB) in version 9.4 in 2014, and most major databases now support querying and indexing JSON data natively, treating it as a first-class storage format rather than just text passing through.

aboveFold.crackTimeNote: Illustrative order-of-magnitude estimates, not guarantees — real security depends entirely on how slowly the service storing this password hashes it, which this tool has no way to know.

rows.text: Prioritize length over complexity — a long passphrase beats a short, symbol-stuffed password.
Allow at least 64 characters; don't cap length short.
Screen new passwords against known-breached password lists.
Force periodic password expiration/rotation on a schedule.
Require a mix of uppercase, symbols, and digits by policy.
Use security questions (mother's maiden name, etc.) as a fallback.

errors.noCharset: Select at least one character type.

intro.title: How Password Strength Actually Works
intro.paragraph1: A password's real strength is its entropy — how many possible passwords an attacker would have to search through before finding yours, expressed in bits (each added bit doubles the search space). It's a function of two things multiplied together: how large the pool of possible characters (or words) is, and how many of them you use. A 12-character password using only lowercase letters has less entropy than an 8-character one mixing upper, lower, numbers, and symbols — length matters, but so does what you draw from.
intro.paragraph2: That's exactly why this tool's passphrase mode exists alongside character-based passwords: four random words from a pool of about 1,650 gives roughly 43 bits of entropy — more than a typical 8-character mixed password — while staying genuinely easier to type and remember. A password's raw entropy tells you how long a brute-force search takes on average, but nothing about entropy is theoretical here: this tool computes the real bit count for exactly what it just generated, shown alongside crack-time estimates for a few realistic attack scenarios below.

diagram.caption: Estimated crack time by composition, at a fixed 100-billion-guesses/second offline attack rate — length and unpredictability both matter, but not equally.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: Five compositions and the exact entropy and crack-time math behind each — the same formula this tool applies live to whatever it just generated for you.

items.question: Is a random string of characters always stronger than a passphrase?
items.answer: Not necessarily — it depends purely on total entropy, not which category it came from. A short 8-character random password and a 4-word passphrase can land at similar bit counts; the passphrase is usually easier to type correctly and remember without writing down, which matters for real-world security since a written-down password defeats its own purpose.

items.question: Why does this tool show a range of crack times instead of one number?
items.answer: Because the true answer depends entirely on something this tool can't see: how the receiving service stores your password. A properly slow hash like bcrypt or Argon2 might allow only thousands of guesses per second even on capable hardware, while a poorly implemented system using fast, unsalted hashing could allow a single GPU to attempt hundreds of billions per second — the same password's real-world safety differs by many orders of magnitude between those two cases.

items.question: Is this tool's random number generator actually secure?
items.answer: Yes — it uses the Web Crypto API's crypto.getRandomValues(), a cryptographically secure random source built into every modern browser, with rejection sampling to avoid the subtle bias a naive modulo operation would introduce. It deliberately does not use Math.random(), which is not designed to be unpredictable enough for security purposes.

items.question: Why does NIST no longer recommend forcing regular password changes?
items.answer: Because research on real password databases found that forced periodic rotation mostly makes people choose weaker passwords or make small, predictable tweaks to their existing one (Password1 → Password2) — which is easier for an attacker with the old password to predict than it is for a legitimate user to remember a genuinely new one. Current guidance instead recommends rotating only when a specific compromise is suspected.

items.question: Does this tool check my password against known data breaches?
items.answer: No, deliberately — doing that accurately requires querying an external breach database, which would mean sending at least a hash of your password over the network. Everything in this tool, including password generation and the strength estimate, runs entirely inside your browser with nothing transmitted anywhere.

items.question: What does "excluding ambiguous characters" actually remove?
items.answer: Characters that are easy to misread depending on the font: the digit 0 versus the letter O, the digit 1 versus lowercase l versus uppercase I, and the vertical bar |. It slightly reduces the character pool (and therefore entropy for the same length), which is a fair trade for a password you might need to type from a handwritten note or read off a screen.

history.title: The Rules That Turned Out to Be Wrong
history.paragraph: Nearly every "must contain a number, a symbol, and a capital letter, changed every 90 days" password policy on Earth traces back to a single 2003 NIST document written by manager Bill Burr — guidance he later admitted was based on a 1980s whitepaper about password habits inside one specific organization, not real large-scale data, since almost none existed at the time. In 2017, by then retired, Burr told the Wall Street Journal "Much of what I did I now regret," after researchers analyzing real breached-password databases found his rules pushed people toward predictable patterns like "Password1!" rather than genuinely unpredictable ones.

modernDevelopments.title: From Complexity Rules to "Correct Horse Battery Staple"
modernDevelopments.paragraph: In August 2011, xkcd comic #936 made the entropy math behind this reframing famous: cartoonist Randall Munroe calculated that the "hard to remember, easy to crack" password Tr0ub4dor&3 carries only about 28 bits of entropy, while the plain, memorable phrase "correct horse battery staple" carries roughly 44 — because entropy comes from unpredictability across a large-enough pool, not from forcing specific character types. NIST's own guidance caught up years later: the current SP 800-63B explicitly recommends prioritizing length over composition complexity, allowing at least 64 characters, and dropping forced periodic rotation — a near-complete reversal of Burr's original 2003 rules.

color-palette-generator.title: Color Palette Generator
color-palette-generator.description: Generate complementary, analogous, triadic, and other color harmonies from a base color, with HEX, RGB, and HSL codes ready to copy.

aboveFold.placeholder: Choose a base color and a harmony type to generate a palette.

form.invalidHex: Enter a valid 6-digit hex color, like #3B82F6.

intro.title: How This Tool Works
intro.paragraph1: This tool generates color harmonies by converting your base color to HSL (hue, saturation, lightness) and rotating its hue around the color wheel by fixed angles specific to each harmony type — 180° for a complementary pair, 120° steps for a triadic trio, and so on — while monochromatic instead holds the hue and saturation constant and varies only lightness. All processing happens locally in your browser; no color you enter here is ever sent anywhere.
intro.paragraph2: Each harmony type reflects a different classic color-wheel relationship rooted in centuries-old color theory: complementary colors sit opposite each other for maximum contrast, analogous colors sit next to each other for a naturally cohesive look, and triadic or tetradic colors are evenly spaced around the wheel for balanced variety. None of these rules guarantee a good design on their own — they're a starting point for exploration, not a substitute for a trained eye.

examples.title: Worked Examples

rows.description: The base color plus its opposite, 180° around the wheel.
Three colors 30° apart, neighbors on the wheel.

items.question: What's the difference between HEX, RGB, and HSL?
items.answer: All three describe the same colors, just in different formats. HEX packs red, green, and blue values into a six-digit code widely used in web design (like #3B82F6). RGB spells out those same three values as numbers from 0-255. HSL instead describes a color by hue (position on the color wheel), saturation (intensity), and lightness — which is often more intuitive for adjusting a color's shade without changing its underlying tone, and is exactly what this tool uses internally to build each harmony.

items.question: Which harmony type should I use?
items.answer: It depends on the effect you want. Complementary pairs create strong contrast and are useful for elements that need to stand out, like a call-to-action button. Analogous colors create a calm, cohesive feel suited to backgrounds or gradients. Triadic and tetradic schemes offer more variety while staying balanced, useful for interfaces needing several distinct but harmonious colors. Monochromatic is the safest choice when you want guaranteed consistency, such as shades for hover and active states of a single UI color.

items.question: Why do some generated colors look muddy or clash even though the math says they're harmonious?
items.answer: Color-wheel harmony rules describe relationships between hues, not how a given hue, saturation, and lightness combination will actually look together on a screen or in print. A mathematically correct triadic set can still look unbalanced if one color is much darker or more saturated than the others. Treat these palettes as a starting point to adjust from, not a finished result.

items.question: Is this the same as how a physical, pigment-based color wheel works?
items.answer: No. This tool works in HSL, a model built for light-based color on screens (additive color), where red, green, and blue combine to make white. Traditional painters' color wheels are typically based on subtractive, pigment-based mixing (red, yellow, blue primaries), which follows different relationships. Both are valid systems for their respective mediums, but they don't map onto each other exactly.

items.question: Does this check whether my colors have enough contrast for accessibility?
items.answer: No. Color harmony and contrast accessibility (such as WCAG contrast ratio requirements for text readability) are different concerns — a harmonious pair of colors can still fail accessibility contrast requirements, or vice versa. Check any palette you plan to use for text or interactive elements against accessibility contrast guidelines separately.

history.title: From Newton's Wheel to the Modern Color Model
history.paragraph: The color wheel traces back to Isaac Newton, who in 1666 arranged the spectrum of visible light into a circle to show how colors relate to one another — the first step toward describing color relationships geometrically rather than just by name. Painters and theorists after Newton, including Johann Wolfgang von Goethe and later Albert Munsell, built on this idea with color-harmony rules based on pigment mixing, laying the groundwork for the complementary, analogous, and triadic relationships still taught today. The HSL model this tool uses is a 20th-century reformulation of the same underlying hue-circle concept, adapted specifically for describing light-based color on screens rather than mixed pigment.

modernDevelopments.title: From Painter's Theory to a Web Design Tool
modernDevelopments.paragraph: For most of their history, color-harmony rules were the province of trained painters and designers working with physical pigments or, later, print color systems. The shift to screen-based design introduced HSL and RGB as the working color models for user interfaces, and color-palette generators like this one moved the same centuries-old harmony rules onto an interactive tool, letting anyone without formal color-theory training explore harmonious combinations for a website, app, or brand starting from a single color they already have in mind.

intro.title: How Unit Conversion Actually Works
intro.paragraph1: The metric system converts easily between units for one deliberate reason: every unit in a category is a power of ten away from its neighbors. A kilometer is exactly 1,000 meters, a centimeter is exactly 1/100 of a meter — converting between them is just shifting a decimal point. Imperial and US customary units carry no such pattern, because they weren't designed as a system at all: they accumulated from separate historical trades and crafts, which is why a foot is 12 inches, a yard is 3 feet, and a mile is 5,280 feet — each ratio is a specific number this tool has to store, not a rule you can derive.
intro.paragraph2: Temperature is the one category where even multiplying by a fixed factor doesn't work, because Celsius and Fahrenheit don't share a common zero point — 0°C is the freezing point of water, not "no temperature," so converting requires shifting the scale before rescaling it, not just multiplying. Kelvin is the exception: it's an absolute scale that starts at true zero (no negative temperatures are physically possible), which is exactly why scientific work is done in Kelvin rather than Celsius or Fahrenheit. Rather than making you pick one target unit at a time, this tool shows the value converted into every unit in the category at once, since "which unit do I actually want" is often the real question.

diagram.caption: Metric prefixes are exact powers of ten apart — converting from kilo to milli is a shift of six decimal places, not a lookup table.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: Five worked examples across different categories, showing the exact inputs and results.

items.question: Why is converting between metric units so much easier than imperial units?
items.answer: Because every metric unit in a category is a power of ten away from its neighbors — a kilometer is always 1,000 meters, no matter the category. Imperial units carry no such pattern: a foot is 12 inches, a yard is 3 feet, a mile is 5,280 feet — each ratio is a separate historical accident with no shared rule, so it has to be looked up rather than derived.

items.question: Why isn't temperature conversion as simple as multiplying by a factor?
items.answer: Because Celsius and Fahrenheit don't share a common zero point — 0°C is the freezing point of water, an arbitrary reference, not an absence of temperature. Converting between them requires shifting the scale by an offset before rescaling, not just multiplying. Kelvin is the one true absolute scale: it starts at absolute zero, the physical limit below which temperature cannot go, which is why it needs no negative numbers and no offset to convert to or from.

items.question: Which countries still don't officially use the metric system?
items.answer: Just three: the United States, Liberia, and Myanmar. All three have legally recognized the metric system for trade and science, but continue using customary units in daily life — the US, notably, made metric the "preferred system" for trade and commerce back in 1988 without ever mandating it domestically.

items.question: What's the difference between a "short ton," a "long ton," and a "metric ton"?
items.answer: A US short ton is 2,000 lb, a British long ton is 2,240 lb, and a metric tonne is 1,000 kg — about 2,204.6 lb. All three get shortened to just "ton" in casual speech, which is exactly how shipping and freight contracts end up in expensive disputes over which one was meant.

items.question: Why is a US gallon smaller than a UK (imperial) gallon?
items.answer: The US kept the older 231-cubic-inch "Queen Anne" wine gallon it inherited before independence, while Britain standardized a new, larger gallon in 1824 defined as the volume of exactly 10 pounds of water. The US never adopted that later British standard, so a US gallon (≈3.785 L) stayed about 20% smaller than a UK gallon (≈4.546 L) — which is why a US car's fuel economy in miles per gallon isn't directly comparable to a UK one's.

items.question: Is a nautical mile the same as a regular mile?
items.answer: No — a nautical mile (used for sea and air travel, and the basis for "knots") is about 1.852 km, versus 1.609 km for a statute (land) mile. A nautical mile isn't an arbitrary number either: it's defined as one minute of latitude along the Earth's meridian, which makes it directly useful for reading a ship or aircraft's position off a map's latitude scale.

history.title: A Decimal System Born From Revolution
history.paragraph: The metric system wasn't a gradual accumulation of trade customs like the units it replaced — it was deliberately designed in a few years. After the French Revolution swept away thousands of inconsistent regional units in 1789, the French Academy of Sciences was tasked in 1791 with defining a rational system based on multiples of ten. It settled on the meter as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the Equator along the meridian through Paris, and sent astronomers Jean-Baptiste Delambre and Pierre Méchain on a multi-year survey expedition to measure that exact distance. France formally adopted the resulting metric system in 1795, and it has been the basis of the world's dominant measurement system ever since.

modernDevelopments.title: From a Platinum Cylinder to a Universal Constant
modernDevelopments.paragraph: For over a century, the kilogram was defined by a single physical object — a platinum-iridium cylinder locked in a vault outside Paris, nicknamed "Le Grand K" — meaning the entire world's mass measurements ultimately traced back to one artifact that could theoretically be damaged, contaminated, or lost. On May 20, 2019, that changed: the kilogram (along with the ampere, kelvin, and mole) was redefined in terms of a fixed fundamental constant of nature — the Planck constant — rather than any physical object. Every unit in the modern SI system can now, in principle, be reproduced anywhere in the universe with the right equipment, with no trip to a vault in France required.

intro.title: How QR Codes Actually Work
intro.paragraph1: A QR code encodes data as a grid of black and white squares called modules, but what makes it scannable from any angle — sideways, upside down, at a distance — is three identical bullseye squares in three of its four corners. A scanner locates those three finder patterns first, which is enough to work out the code's rotation and perspective before it even starts reading the data in between.
intro.paragraph2: The data itself is protected by Reed-Solomon error correction, the same family of algorithm used to protect CDs, DVDs, and deep-space transmissions from NASA probes. The encoder stores extra, redundant codewords alongside the real data, spread across the grid — which is exactly what lets a QR code stay scannable even with a logo covering its center or a corner torn off. This tool's four error-correction levels (L through H) trade code density for exactly how much damage the result can survive.

items.question: Why can a QR code be scanned from any angle, even upside down?
items.answer: Because of the three identical bullseye "finder patterns" in three of its four corners. A scanner locates those first, and their fixed, asymmetric arrangement is enough to calculate the code's rotation and perspective before it reads any of the actual data in between.

items.question: Why doesn't putting a logo in the middle of a QR code break it?
items.answer: Because of Reed-Solomon error correction — the same family of algorithm that protects CDs, DVDs, and deep-space spacecraft transmissions from damage. The encoder weaves redundant recovery data throughout the grid, so a scanner can reconstruct the missing or covered part as long as the damage stays within the chosen error-correction level's threshold (7% to 30%, depending on the level picked).

items.question: What's the difference between a static and a dynamic QR code?
items.answer: A static QR code — what this tool generates — encodes your actual content directly, so it can never be edited or tracked, but it also never expires or depends on a third-party service staying online. A dynamic QR code instead encodes a short redirect URL you control, letting you change the destination or see scan counts later, at the cost of relying on that redirect service indefinitely.

items.question: Is it safe to scan any QR code?
items.answer: Not automatically — a technique known as "quishing" (QR phishing) relies on people scanning unsolicited codes (stuck over a legitimate one on a parking meter, for instance) straight into a fake login page. Most phone cameras show a URL preview before opening a link from a QR code; it's worth actually reading it, the same way you'd check a link before clicking it in an email.

items.question: How much data can a QR code actually hold?
items.answer: The largest QR code version (Version 40, a 177×177 grid) can hold up to 7,089 numeric digits or 4,296 alphanumeric characters at the lowest error-correction level — though most real-world QR codes use a small fraction of that, since a URL or a Wi-Fi password rarely needs thousands of characters, and a denser code is slower and less reliable to scan.

items.question: Why are QR code payments so much more common in China and India than in the US or Europe?
items.answer: Largely because those markets went mobile-first: platforms like Alipay, WeChat Pay, and India's UPI rolled out QR-based payments at a moment when card-payment infrastructure (point-of-sale terminals) was still far less widespread than in markets that had already built out card networks for decades — a QR code printed on a piece of paper is dramatically cheaper to deploy than a card terminal, so it became the default rather than a card-network alternative.

history.title: From Toyota's Assembly Line to Your Pocket
history.paragraph: QR codes were invented in 1994 by a small team led by engineer Masahiro Hara at Denso Wave, a Toyota Group subsidiary, to solve a specific factory problem: standard barcodes could only hold about 20 characters, nowhere near enough to track the growing complexity of automotive parts on the assembly line. Hara's team designed a two-dimensional code that could store over 4,000 characters, be read from any angle, and stay scannable even partially damaged — then Denso Wave made the decision that turned it into a global standard rather than a proprietary factory tool: it patented the invention but chose never to enforce the patent, making the format free for anyone to use.

modernDevelopments.title: From Factory Floors to Restaurant Tables
modernDevelopments.paragraph: For most of QR codes' first 25 years, they stayed a mostly Asian phenomenon, driven by mobile-payment platforms like Alipay and WeChat Pay. That changed almost overnight in 2020, when contactless restaurant menus and check-in forms made QR codes a daily habit worldwide during the COVID-19 pandemic — global scan volume roughly tripled within a year. The other major modern shift is dynamic QR codes: instead of encoding a destination directly, they encode a short redirect link a business can repoint later without reprinting a single code, and can track how many times it was scanned.

intro.title: How Barcodes Actually Work
intro.paragraph1: A 1D barcode encodes data purely as the widths of alternating bars and spaces — there's no color, no dots, nothing two-dimensional about it. A scanner's laser or camera sensor sweeps across the code and measures how long the light stays bright or dark at each point; a narrow bar might be one "module" wide, a wide one three or four modules wide, and the exact sequence of those widths is what encodes each digit or character. This is also exactly why 1D barcodes carry no error correction the way a QR code does: there's no spare redundant data woven in to reconstruct a damaged section, which is why this tool places an optional logo beside the barcode rather than on top of it.
intro.paragraph2: UPC-A and EAN-13 add one more safeguard: a check digit, mathematically derived from every other digit in the code, that a scanner recalculates after reading and compares against — if a smudge or printing defect corrupted even one digit, the check digit almost certainly won't match, and the scanner rejects the read instead of accepting corrupted data. Code 128 goes further with a full checksum symbol computed from every character's value. This tool calculates every check digit and checksum for you automatically from whatever value you enter.

items.question: Can I actually use this barcode to sell a product in stores?
items.answer: Not on its own. Any UPC-A or EAN-13 number you make up yourself may already belong to a different product somewhere in the world — retailers and marketplaces require a number properly issued through GS1 (or your country's equivalent numbering authority), which guarantees it's uniquely yours. This tool is for education, design mockups, internal tracking, and anywhere a globally unique registered number isn't required.

items.question: Why can't I put a logo directly on top of the barcode lines?
items.answer: Unlike a QR code, a 1D barcode has no error-correction redundancy at all — every bar and space is load-bearing. Covering even a small part of the code can make specific digits unreadable, and a scanner has no spare data to reconstruct what's missing. That's exactly why this tool only offers to place a logo beside the code, never over it.

items.question: What's the actual difference between UPC-A and EAN-13?
items.answer: EAN-13 is really UPC-A's superset: encode a UPC-A number as EAN-13 by adding a leading 0, and it decodes identically. UPC-A (12 digits) is the historical US/Canada retail standard; EAN-13 (13 digits) is the international standard used almost everywhere else, including by products sold in the US, since American scanners read EAN-13 too.

items.question: Why does Code 128 look so different from UPC-A or EAN-13?
items.answer: Because it solves a different problem. UPC-A and EAN-13 exist purely to encode a specific numeric product identifier for retail checkout. Code 128 can encode letters, punctuation, and digits in one code, at any length, which is why it's the default choice for shipping labels, warehouse pallet IDs, and internal tracking codes rather than retail products.

items.question: Why does the barcode need a check digit or checksum at all?
items.answer: Because printing and scanning aren't perfect — a smudge, a fold, or a low-quality printer can corrupt part of a code. The check digit is calculated from every other digit using a fixed formula; if a scanner reads a corrupted code, the digit it reads almost certainly won't match what the formula predicts, so it rejects the scan instead of ringing up the wrong product.

items.question: Is my data uploaded anywhere when I use this tool, including the logo?
items.answer: No — encoding the barcode and placing an uploaded logo image both happen entirely inside your browser. Nothing you enter or upload here is transmitted anywhere.

history.title: A 1949 Patent for Concentric Circles
history.paragraph: The barcode's origin story starts with an overheard conversation: in 1948, graduate student Bernard Silver overheard a supermarket executive asking a Drexel Institute dean for a way to automatically read product information at checkout. Silver teamed up with fellow student Norman Joseph Woodland, who — drawing on Morse code he'd learned as a Boy Scout — sketched an early design using dots and dashes, then reworked it into a pattern of concentric circles so it could be scanned from any direction. They filed a patent in 1949, granted in 1952, and sold it to Philco for just $15,000 — genuinely the only money either inventor made directly from an idea that would go on to reshape global retail.

modernDevelopments.title: From a Bullseye to a Pack of Gum
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Woodland and Silver's original concentric-circle design was never mass-produced — the linear barcode actually used today was designed separately, starting in 1969, by IBM engineer George Laurer, who (with Woodland, by then also at IBM, and mathematician David Savir) proposed the striped Universal Product Code adopted by the US grocery industry's Symbol Selection Committee in 1973. The first UPC-scanned retail sale happened on June 26, 1974, when a pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum was rung up at a Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio. Europe adopted a compatible 13-digit extension, EAN, in 1976, and the two standards are now governed globally by GS1 — formed in 2005 from the merger of the original US and European numbering authorities.

intro.title: How Word Counting Actually Works
intro.paragraph1: Behind a single 'word count' number are several separate, deliberate decisions about what counts as a word, a sentence, and a paragraph. A word counter first tokenizes raw text — splitting it into individual units on whitespace and punctuation boundaries — then classifies those tokens: runs of characters ending in '.', '!', or '?' close out a sentence; blank lines mark paragraph breaks; and every token is measured for length and compared against every other token to find unique words and the longest one. None of this is guesswork once the rules are fixed, but the rules themselves are a choice, which is exactly why two different tools can report two different counts for the same text.
intro.paragraph2: Reading-time estimates add one more layer: a words-per-minute (WPM) constant, multiplied against the word count. This tool uses 200 WPM, a commonly cited middle-of-the-road figure for adult silent reading of English prose; a large 2019 meta-analysis of reading-speed research (see the reference below) puts the actual average closer to 238 WPM for non-fiction, with wide variation by reader, language, and text difficulty — which is why any reading-time estimate should be read as a reasonable approximation, not a precise measurement. Keyword density, this tool's third layer, works by counting how often each word recurs after filtering out short, high-frequency function words ('the', 'and', 'of') so that what's left reflects the text's actual subject matter rather than its grammar.

items.question: Why does my word count here differ from what my word processor shows?
items.answer: Different tools use different tokenization rules — some count a hyphenated compound as one word, others as two; some count numbers or standalone punctuation as words, others don't. There is no single universal standard, so small discrepancies between tools counting the exact same text are normal and expected.

items.question: What exactly counts as a sentence or a paragraph here?
items.answer: A sentence is any run of text ending in a period, exclamation mark, or question mark (or the final unterminated fragment, if your text doesn't end with one). A paragraph is any block of text separated from the next by one or more blank lines. Neither rule understands abbreviations like 'Mr.' or 'e.g.', so text dense with those may show a slightly inflated sentence count.

items.question: Is the reading-time estimate the same as speaking or presentation time?
items.answer: No. This estimate is calibrated to silent reading speed (roughly 200 words per minute), which is meaningfully faster than speaking pace — spoken presentations typically run closer to 130–150 words per minute, so a script that reads as a 3-minute read here would take noticeably longer to actually deliver out loud.

items.question: Why are common words like "the" and "and" left out of the top keywords list?
items.answer: Because those short, high-frequency function words appear constantly in any text regardless of topic, so including them would make every keyword list look identical. Filtering them out — a standard technique called stopword removal — leaves behind the words that actually distinguish what your text is about.

items.question: Does this tool store, upload, or share the text I type?
items.answer: No — every statistic here, including the keyword ranking, is computed directly in your browser as you type. Your text is never sent to a server or stored anywhere.

items.question: Why do character limits matter for things like X posts or meta descriptions?
items.answer: Platforms and search engines enforce hard or soft character caps for structural reasons: an SMS segment tops out at 160 characters for network protocol reasons, a Google search snippet truncates meta descriptions around 155–160 characters, and X caps posts at 280 characters by product design. Writing past these limits means your text gets cut off, truncated with an ellipsis, or rejected outright — so checking your count against the actual target platform before publishing avoids that.

history.title: Counting Words Before Computers Did It
history.paragraph: Word counts mattered commercially long before software existed to compute them: 19th- and early-20th-century magazine and newspaper publishers commonly paid writers by the word, which made an accurate manual word count a direct financial matter for both author and editor, and pulp fiction and serialized novelists — including some of the era's most famous writers — were acutely aware of their per-installment word totals for exactly that reason. Formal readability research followed in the mid-20th century, most notably Rudolf Flesch's 1948 reading-ease formula, which combined average sentence length and syllable counts into a single score — establishing sentence and word length as measurable, comparable properties of a text rather than just a stylistic impression.

modernDevelopments.title: From Manual Tallies to Real-Time Computational Text Analysis
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Modern text analysis has extended far beyond simple counts into corpus linguistics — the large-scale computational study of word frequency and usage patterns across huge collections of real text — which now underpins everything from dictionary compilation to search-engine ranking to the keyword-density tools writers use for search-engine optimization. Real-time, in-browser word counting, the kind this tool performs as you type, became broadly practical only once client-side JavaScript execution became fast enough to re-tokenize and re-analyze full documents on every keystroke without noticeable lag — a routine capability today, but a nontrivial one as recently as the early web.

intro.title: How Base64 Encoding Actually Works
intro.paragraph1: Base64 solves one narrow problem: representing arbitrary binary data — the raw bytes of an image, a file, or any content that isn't plain text — using only characters that are guaranteed to survive being passed through text-only channels like email bodies, URLs, or JSON strings. It does this by regrouping data. Binary data is naturally organized into 8-bit bytes, but Base64 reads it in chunks of three bytes (24 bits) at a time and regroups those same 24 bits into four 6-bit groups instead. Since 6 bits can represent exactly 64 distinct values (2⁶ = 64), each 6-bit group maps directly onto one of 64 printable characters — hence the name.
intro.paragraph2: This regrouping is also exactly why Base64 output is always about a third larger than the original input: three input bytes (24 bits) become four output characters, and since each output character is stored as one full byte of text even though it only carries 6 bits of actual information, the encoded result inflates by a factor of 4/3, or roughly 33%. When the input length isn't a clean multiple of three bytes, standard Base64 pads the output with one or two '=' characters so the decoder can tell exactly how many of the final group's bits are real data versus filler — the URL-safe variant this tool also supports typically omits that padding entirely, since it's most often used in contexts (like URLs) where a trailing '=' would need its own escaping anyway.

diagram.caption: Base64's core regrouping: three 8-bit bytes (24 bits total) are read as one continuous bit stream and split into four 6-bit groups instead, each of which maps to one printable Base64 character.
