items.question: Why does encoding make my data about 33% larger?
items.answer: Because Base64 spends one full output character to carry only 6 bits of real information, while a plain byte carries 8. Three input bytes (24 bits) always become four output characters — a 4-for-3 expansion, which works out to roughly 33% overhead regardless of what the original data was.

items.question: What's actually different between standard and URL-safe Base64?
items.answer: Only two characters change: standard Base64 uses '+' and '/' in its alphabet, while URL-safe Base64 (defined in RFC 4648 §5) replaces them with '-' and '_' — both characters that don't need escaping inside a URL or filename. URL-safe output also typically omits the trailing '=' padding for the same reason. Everything else about the encoding is identical.

items.question: Is Base64 a form of encryption or a security measure?
items.answer: No — Base64 provides zero confidentiality. It's a reversible, publicly documented encoding with no key involved, so anyone can decode it in one step with any Base64 tool, including this one. It's meant purely to make binary data transportable through text-only channels, never to hide or protect it.

items.question: Why do I sometimes see trailing '=' characters and sometimes not?
items.answer: The '=' characters are padding, added only when the input length isn't an exact multiple of 3 bytes, so the decoder knows precisely how many bits in the final group are real data. One '=' means the last group encoded 2 real bytes; two '=' means it encoded 1. Input lengths that are already a multiple of 3 need no padding at all — and the URL-safe variant omits it by convention regardless.

items.question: Does the file panel upload my file anywhere?
items.answer: No — the file is read directly in your browser using the File API, and the resulting Base64 data URI is generated and displayed locally. Nothing is ever uploaded to a server.

items.question: Why does decoding sometimes fail with an "invalid Base64" error even though the text looks fine?
items.answer: Standard Base64 requires the input length to be an exact multiple of 4 characters and every character to come from its specific 64-character alphabet; a single stray character, wrong padding, or mixing the standard and URL-safe alphabets (for example, decoding a '+' as URL-safe) will all correctly fail rather than silently produce garbage.

history.title: Getting Binary Data Through Text-Only Pipes
history.paragraph: The core problem Base64 solves predates it by decades: early Unix systems used uuencode, introduced around 1980, to pack binary files into the plain-ASCII format that Unix-to-Unix Copy (UUCP) mail transfers required. The specific Base64 scheme in use today emerged with MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions), formalized by Nathaniel Borenstein and Ned Freed in RFC 1521 in 1993, which needed a reliable way to attach binary files — images, documents, executables — to email messages built on a protocol (SMTP) originally designed to carry only 7-bit ASCII text.

modernDevelopments.title: From Email Attachments to Web-Native Tokens
modernDevelopments.paragraph: RFC 4648, published in 2006, generalized and formally standardized Base64 (alongside Base16 and Base32) independent of its original email context, explicitly defining the URL-safe and filename-safe variant this tool supports. Base64 is now everywhere on the modern web well beyond email: data URIs let small images and fonts be embedded directly inside HTML or CSS to save an extra HTTP request; HTTP Basic Authentication headers carry credentials Base64-encoded (not encrypted); and JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) — the standard for modern web authentication — encode their header, payload, and signature segments using exactly the URL-safe, unpadded Base64 variant this tool's toggle produces.

intro.title: How CSV and JSON Actually Relate
intro.paragraph1: CSV and JSON solve the same basic problem — representing a list of records — with opposite structural assumptions. CSV assumes every record has exactly the same flat set of fields, so it only needs to write the field names once, in a header row, then just the values afterward. JSON makes no such assumption: every object carries its own keys, which is what lets it represent records with different shapes, or fields that are themselves nested objects and arrays, at the cost of repeating those key names in every single record.
intro.paragraph2: That structural gap is exactly why CSV → JSON is mechanical (each row becomes an object, each header becomes a key) while JSON → CSV requires real decisions this tool makes automatically: nested objects get flattened into dot-notation columns (address.city, address.zip), and arrays get serialized as a single JSON-text cell, since CSV has no native way to represent a list inside a list.

diagram.caption: A CSV header row becomes JSON object keys; each subsequent CSV row becomes one JSON object in an array.

items.question: Why would I choose CSV over JSON, or the other way around?
items.answer: CSV wins for flat, tabular data — a spreadsheet export, a list of contacts — because it's smaller and every spreadsheet program opens it natively. JSON wins the moment your data has real structure — nested objects, fields that are themselves lists — because CSV simply has no native way to represent that without flattening or stringifying it, which this tool does automatically but always loses a little structural clarity in the process.

items.question: What happens to nested objects when converting JSON to CSV?
items.answer: They get flattened into dot-notation column names — a nested { "address": { "city": "Cairo" } } becomes a column literally named address.city. This keeps every value in its own cell, at the cost of a less human-friendly header row for deeply nested data.

items.question: What happens to arrays when converting JSON to CSV?
items.answer: Unlike nested objects, arrays get serialized as JSON text inside a single cell — CSV has no native concept of "a list inside a list," so there's no clean tabular alternative. The result round-trips correctly (converting back to JSON restores the original array), but isn't especially readable in a spreadsheet.

items.question: Why does auto-detecting the delimiter matter?
items.answer: Comma-separated is the default, but it's genuinely not universal: many European locales use a comma as the decimal separator, so spreadsheet software there exports CSV with semicolons instead to avoid ambiguity, and tab- or pipe-delimited exports are common from certain databases and legacy systems. Auto-detect looks at the first line and picks whichever candidate delimiter appears most often.

items.question: Why does this tool need a "first row is a header" option?
items.answer: Not every CSV file includes one — some raw database or sensor-log exports start directly with data. Without a real header to draw keys from, this tool falls back to generic column1, column2, ... keys so the conversion still produces valid, usable JSON.

items.question: Is my data uploaded anywhere when I use this tool?
items.answer: No — parsing and converting both directions happens entirely in your browser. Nothing you paste here is transmitted anywhere, which matters since CSV and JSON files often carry real exported data.

history.title: A Format With No Single Inventor
history.paragraph: Unlike JSON, CSV has no known creator and no founding date — it emerged organically because separating values with commas was simply the most obvious way to represent tabular data in early computing, with IBM's Fortran compiler already supporting a comma-delimited format as far back as 1972. The term "comma-separated values" itself only entered common use around 1983. For over three decades, every piece of software that read or wrote CSV files quietly invented its own conventions for the genuinely tricky edge cases — what happens when a value itself contains a comma, or a line break, or a quote mark — which is exactly why real-world CSV files remain inconsistent to this day.

modernDevelopments.title: A Standard, Decades Late
modernDevelopments.paragraph: The first attempt to formally document CSV's de facto conventions didn't arrive until October 2005, when Yakov Shafranovich published RFC 4180, codifying rules for quoting, escaping, and header rows that most implementations had already converged on independently. It's explicitly an "Informational" RFC, not a binding standard, and it arrived roughly three decades after CSV files were already common — which is why this tool's own CSV parser has to handle real-world files that don't strictly follow it, rather than assuming every file will.

intro.title: How This Tool Works
intro.paragraph1: This tool reads and writes PDF files entirely inside your browser, using the same underlying document structure that PDF readers use internally: a PDF is a collection of pages, each an independent object, alongside a set of fonts, images, and other resources they reference. Merging simply copies every page object from each source file, in order, into a new document; splitting copies a chosen subset of page objects into one or more new documents. No file you upload here is ever sent to a server — everything happens locally on your device.
intro.paragraph2: Because this all runs in your browser's memory, very large files or a very large number of files can slow down or strain the page. This tool caps the total size of files processed in a single operation at 25 MB, a limit chosen to keep processing fast and reliable across a wide range of devices rather than an arbitrary restriction.

A 25 MB total limit keeps the tool fast and reliable for the vast majority of everyday documents while protecting your browsing experience.

items.answer: No. This tool works with standard, unencrypted PDF files. Password-protected or corrupted files may fail to load; you would need to remove the password or repair the file with dedicated software before merging or splitting it here.

history.title: From a Proprietary Format to a Universal Standard
history.paragraph: PDF was created by Adobe Systems in 1993 as the Portable Document Format, designed to let a document look identical regardless of what software, hardware, or operating system opened it — a genuinely hard problem at a time when word processors routinely mangled each other's formatting. Adobe initially kept the format proprietary and sold viewer software, but released the specification openly in the early 2000s, and PDF became an official ISO international standard (ISO 32000) in 2008, cementing it as a truly cross-platform, vendor-neutral format rather than one tied to a single company's software.

modernDevelopments.title: From Specialized Software to a Browser Tab
modernDevelopments.paragraph: For most of PDF's history, merging or splitting documents required desktop software — dedicated PDF editors, printer drivers that could combine print jobs, or command-line tools understood mainly by developers. Modern web browsers now include JavaScript engines fast enough to parse and rewrite PDF's internal page-object structure directly, which is what libraries like the one behind this tool rely on, making an operation that once required installed software into something that runs in an ordinary browser tab, with no upload and no installation.

intro.title: How This Tool Works
intro.paragraph1: This tool compresses and extracts ZIP archives entirely inside your browser using the DEFLATE algorithm, the same lossless compression method built into the ZIP format since its creation. Compressing packs each file's bytes, shrunk using DEFLATE, into a single archive alongside a directory listing every file's name and location; extracting reads that directory and reverses the compression to recover each file's original bytes exactly. No file you add here is ever sent to a server — everything happens locally on your device.
intro.paragraph2: Because all of this runs in your browser's memory, very large files or a very large number of files can slow down or strain the page. This tool caps the total size processed in a single operation at 50 MB, a limit chosen to keep compression and extraction fast and reliable across a wide range of devices rather than an arbitrary restriction.

A 50 MB total limit keeps the tool fast and reliable for the vast majority of everyday files while protecting your browsing experience.

history.title: From an Information Theory Paper to a File Format
history.paragraph: The compression technique underlying ZIP traces back to a 1977 paper by Abraham Lempel and Jacob Ziv describing a general-purpose method for compressing sequential data by replacing repeated patterns with shorter references to where they appeared before — an approach now called LZ77. Roughly a decade later, developer Phil Katz combined a refinement of this idea with Huffman coding, another compression technique, into the DEFLATE algorithm and released it as the core of the ZIP file format in 1989, specifically designing it to be implementable without infringing on then-existing patents covering a competing compression method.

modernDevelopments.title: From a DOS Utility to a Universal Standard
modernDevelopments.paragraph: ZIP began as PKZIP, a DOS command-line utility, but its specification was published openly rather than kept proprietary, which let it become the de facto standard archive format across essentially every operating system and platform. Modern web browsers now include JavaScript engines fast enough to implement DEFLATE compression and decompression directly, which is what libraries like the one behind this tool rely on, making an operation that once required installed software into something that runs in an ordinary browser tab, with no upload and no installation.

intro.title: Why File Size Conversion Isn't as Simple as It Looks
intro.paragraph1: There are actually two different, equally legitimate definitions of "kilobyte" in everyday use, and they disagree by more than 2%. The decimal (SI) definition treats "kilo" the same way it's used everywhere else in science — exactly 1,000 — so 1 KB = 1,000 bytes, 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes, and so on. The binary definition instead uses powers of 2, since computer memory is addressed in binary: 1 KB = 2¹⁰ = 1,024 bytes, 1 MB = 2²⁰ = 1,048,576 bytes. Both are real, both are still in active use today, and neither is simply 'wrong' — they're answering different questions about how the underlying hardware works.
intro.paragraph2: The practical problem is that the gap between these two standards compounds at every step up the scale. It starts small — 1,024 is only 2.4% larger than 1,000 — but that difference multiplies at each higher unit: by the terabyte level it has grown to roughly 10%, which is exactly why a drive advertised and sold as "1 TB" (the decimal definition, matching its true manufactured capacity) shows up in an operating system reporting free space in binary units as only about 931 GB — no storage has vanished; the OS is measuring in a different-sized "gigabyte" than the one printed on the box.

diagram.caption: The gap between binary (1024-based) and decimal (1000-based) units at each order of magnitude — starting at 2.4% for kilo and compounding to nearly 12.6% by peta.

items.question: Why does my "1 TB" hard drive show up as only about 931 GB in Windows?
items.answer: Because the drive's advertised capacity is measured in the decimal standard (1 TB = 1,000,000,000,000 bytes, matching its true physical capacity), while Windows' File Explorer reports free space using binary-based math but decimal-looking unit labels. The same byte count, read in true binary GiB units, is a smaller number — no capacity is actually missing.

items.question: What's the actual difference between KB and KiB?
items.answer: KB (kilobyte) is the decimal unit, always meaning exactly 1,000 bytes under the modern IEC/NIST-recommended naming. KiB (kibibyte) is the binary unit, always meaning exactly 1,024 bytes. The two-letter "i" in KiB, MiB, GiB, and so on exists specifically to make this distinction unambiguous — a convention this tool follows in its binary-standard column.

items.question: Which standard should I actually use — decimal or binary?
items.answer: It depends what you're measuring. Storage capacity (hard drives, SSDs, flash drives) and network bandwidth are conventionally quoted in decimal units by manufacturers and ISPs. RAM capacity is inherently binary, since memory is physically addressed in powers of 2, which is why RAM sizes (8 GB, 16 GB, 32 GB) are quietly binary values even though they're labeled with decimal-looking unit names.

items.question: Why do storage manufacturers use decimal while operating systems often show binary?
items.answer: Decimal units make a drive's true capacity look larger and align with the SI system used for every other physical quantity, which is a genuine commercial incentive as well as a technically defensible choice. Operating systems, on the other hand, evolved from a computing culture where memory addressing was always binary, so many (Windows especially) still compute in binary internally — they just haven't updated their on-screen unit labels to match, which is the direct source of the mismatch.

items.question: Does this decimal-vs-binary confusion affect network speeds too?
items.answer: Network and internet connection speeds are always quoted in decimal bits per second (Mbps, Gbps) — never binary — and bits are not the same unit as the bytes file sizes are measured in. That's a second, separate source of confusion: an 8 megabit-per-second connection transfers only about 1 megabyte per second, not 8, because there are 8 bits in a byte.

items.question: Why might this tool's download-time estimate differ from what I see in an actual browser or app?
items.answer: This estimate assumes a constant, uninterrupted connection running at exactly the stated link speed, converting the file's byte size to bits and dividing by that speed. Real transfers are affected by network overhead, other traffic sharing the connection, server-side throttling, and the gap between a connection's theoretical maximum speed and what it actually sustains — so treat this as a best-case estimate, not a guarantee.

history.title: A Convenient Shorthand That Outgrew Its Convenience
history.paragraph: Computer memory has always been addressed in powers of two, so early computer scientists in the 1960s and 1970s noticed that 2¹⁰ (1,024) happened to land conveniently close to 1,000 and started informally borrowing the SI prefix "kilo" to describe it — a shorthand of convenience, not a formal standard. That informal reuse spread through the industry for decades with no single body regulating it, so "kilobyte" quietly came to mean two different numbers depending on context, a discrepancy small enough at the kilobyte scale to go largely unnoticed but destined to compound as storage capacities grew into the megabyte, gigabyte, and eventually terabyte range.

modernDevelopments.title: A Formal Standard That the Industry Still Hasn't Fully Adopted
modernDevelopments.paragraph: The International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) formally resolved the ambiguity by introducing distinct binary prefixes — kibi, mebi, gibi, and beyond — first in IEC 60027-2 in 1998 and consolidated in IEC 80000-13:2008, the standard this tool's binary-unit column follows. NIST and most standards bodies now officially recommend this distinction. Adoption remains uneven in practice, however: Linux distributions and Apple's macOS/iOS have largely switched storage displays to true decimal units to match manufacturer specifications, while Windows still displays binary-computed values under decimal-looking labels — which is precisely the mismatch this tool's side-by-side comparison is built to make visible.

intro.title: Why File Names Need Sanitizing at All
intro.paragraph1: A file name isn't just a label — on most operating systems, it's also data the file system's own command interpreter can parse, which is exactly why certain characters are forbidden. A forward slash or backslash means a path separator, a colon can mean a drive letter or an alternate data stream, and a question mark or asterisk means a wildcard pattern — so a file literally named "invoice?.pdf" would be ambiguous or outright rejected by the very systems meant to store it. Sanitizing a file name means stripping or replacing exactly these structurally meaningful characters, while leaving everything else about the name intact.
intro.paragraph2: Beyond individual characters, whole file names can be reserved outright: Windows blocks CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, and the numbered COM and LPT ports as file names, in any case and with or without an extension, because these strings are historically bound to physical devices at the operating-system level, not to the file system. A file name ending in a dot or space is silently stripped by Windows' own APIs, which can create confusing mismatches between what a user types and what actually gets saved. This tool's "what changed" report exists specifically to make each of these otherwise invisible corrections visible.

diagram.caption: The sanitization pipeline: a raw file name is normalized (illegal characters and whitespace handled), checked against reserved names and length limits, and only then considered safe to use everywhere.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: How different problem file names get resolved.

items.question: Why replace spaces with dashes instead of just removing them?
items.answer: Removing spaces entirely would merge words together and make the name harder to read ("myfile" instead of "my-file"), while a separator preserves the word boundaries. Dashes and underscores are also both universally safe across every major operating system and are the convention most web upload systems and URLs expect.

items.question: What characters are actually illegal in file names, and why these specific ones?
items.answer: On Windows: < > : " / \ | ? * and any control character (ASCII 0–31). Each one is reserved for a structural reason — / and \ are path separators, : can denote a drive letter, ? and * are wildcard characters in command shells, and < > | are shell redirection and piping operators. macOS and Linux are far more permissive, but this tool sanitizes to the strictest common set so the result is guaranteed safe everywhere.

items.question: Why does "CON.txt" get renamed instead of just cleaned up?
items.answer: Because CON isn't an illegal-character problem — every character in it is perfectly valid. The entire base name is reserved by Windows as an alias for the system console device, regardless of extension or case, so "con.txt", "CON.txt", and even plain "con" are all blocked outright. The only fix is renaming the base name itself, which is why this tool appends a suffix rather than trying to strip anything.

items.question: What's the 255-character limit about, and does it apply to me?
items.answer: 255 is the maximum file name length on most modern file systems (NTFS, ext4, APFS), measured per path component, not the full path. Most everyday file names never come close to this limit, but names auto-generated by exporting long titles, timestamps, or metadata into a file name can occasionally exceed it — this tool truncates while always preserving the extension.

items.question: Why would I want to transliterate accented characters?
items.answer: Accented and non-Latin characters (é, ñ, ü, etc.) are technically valid in modern file names on every major OS, but they can still cause real problems: older tools, certain command-line environments, and some upload or CDN systems handle non-ASCII file names inconsistently or reject them outright. Transliterating to plain ASCII trades a small amount of readability for guaranteed compatibility with the widest possible range of systems.

items.question: Does this tool rename my actual file, or just suggest a new name?
items.answer: This tool only computes and displays what a safe version of the name would look like — it never touches any real file, since everything runs on text you type or paste directly in your browser. You still need to rename the actual file yourself using the suggested result.

history.title: Why "CON" and "PRN" Are Still Forbidden Today
history.paragraph: The reserved device names this tool checks for — CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, and the numbered COM and LPT ports — trace back to early MS-DOS, where the operating system needed a way to let a single command work on either a real file or a physical device: typing "copy report.txt PRN" would send a file straight to the printer, using PRN as a stand-in name for whatever printer device was attached, in exactly the same command syntax used for copying between files. For that redirection trick to work reliably, these device names had to be permanently blocked as file names at the operating-system level, everywhere, so a file could never be confused for a device.

modernDevelopments.title: From 8.3 Names to Long, Unicode-Aware File Systems
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Early DOS file systems (FAT) restricted every file name to the rigid "8.3" format — 8 characters, a dot, and a 3-character extension, uppercase only — which Windows 95's VFAT extension finally lifted in 1995, introducing the long file names and lowercase support taken for granted today. Modern file systems like NTFS and APFS support names up to 255 characters with full Unicode, but the legacy restrictions — the reserved device names, the illegal-character set, the ban on trailing dots — were kept for backward compatibility rather than removed, which is exactly why a modern sanitizer like this one still needs to check for rules that trace back over four decades.

intro.title: How Deduplication Actually Works
intro.paragraph1: The naive way to find duplicates — compare every line against every other line — takes time that grows quadratically with the list's size: doubling a list's length roughly quadruples the comparison work, which becomes impractical past a few thousand lines. A hash-based approach sidesteps this entirely by keeping a running set of every line already seen: for each new line, checking whether it's already in that set takes roughly constant time regardless of how large the set has grown, since a hash function converts the line's content directly into a lookup position rather than requiring a scan. This is exactly why deduplication tools, including this one, can process lists with tens of thousands of lines instantly rather than freezing.
intro.paragraph2: This also explains why the settings on this tool matter more than they might first appear. "Case-sensitive" and "trim whitespace" both control what actually goes into the hash function — turning case-sensitivity off means "Apple" and "apple" hash to the same bucket and collapse into one; trimming whitespace means " apple" and "apple" do the same. "Keep first" versus "keep last" doesn't change which lines are considered duplicates at all — only which single copy of each duplicate group is the one that survives into the output, and where it ends up positioned.

diagram.caption: How hash-based deduplication works: each input line is checked against a running set of lines already seen. A new line is added to both the set and the output; a repeat (struck through) is skipped entirely.

items.question: Why does this tool drop blank lines entirely?
items.answer: Blank lines don't carry any meaningful content to deduplicate — a list of five blank lines isn't five different pieces of data, it's just formatting. Dropping them keeps the output focused purely on actual list items, rather than cluttering it with meaningless empty entries.

items.question: What's actually the difference between "case-sensitive" and "trim whitespace"?
items.answer: Case-sensitivity controls letter casing specifically — whether "Apple" and "apple" are treated as the same line. Trimming whitespace is a separate, independent setting that controls leading and trailing spaces — whether " apple" and "apple" are treated as the same line. You can toggle either one independently of the other.

items.question: Why would I ever want to keep the last occurrence instead of the first?
items.answer: Order often carries meaning: in a chronologically appended log or a list where later entries represent updates or corrections to earlier ones, the most recent occurrence of a repeated key is usually the one you actually want to keep, not the oldest. "Keep last" preserves that intent instead of defaulting to whichever came first.

items.question: Does sorting change which lines are considered duplicates?
items.answer: No — sorting only reorders the already-deduplicated output alphabetically; it happens as a separate step after duplicate detection is complete, and has no effect at all on which lines were identified as repeats or which occurrence was kept.

items.question: Is this tool's line-ending handling reliable across Windows, macOS, and Linux files?
items.answer: Yes — the three common line-ending conventions (\r\n on Windows, \n on macOS/Linux, and the older \r alone) are all recognized and normalized automatically, so pasting a list exported from any of these systems works correctly without manual cleanup.

items.question: Why does the duplicates list show a count next to each repeated line?
items.answer: The count is the total number of times that exact line appeared in your original input, including the one copy that was kept — so a count of 3 means two copies were removed, not three. This makes it possible to spot which values were duplicated most heavily at a glance, not just that duplicates existed somewhere.

history.title: From Punch-Card Sorting to the Hash Table
history.paragraph: Before hash tables existed, finding duplicates in a large dataset meant sorting it first — an approach with roots in mechanical punch-card sorting machines used for census and business data processing in the early-to-mid 20th century, where physically ordering cards made matching records against each other practical at scale. The conceptual breakthrough that made lookup-based deduplication possible arrived with Hans Peter Luhn's internal IBM research in the 1950s on hashing, formally published by his colleague W. W. Peterson in 1957 — introducing the idea of computing a numeric address directly from a piece of data's content, rather than needing to search or sort for it.

modernDevelopments.title: From Punch Cards to Instant Browser-Based Deduplication
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Hashing became a foundational tool across computing well beyond deduplication — it underpins database indexing, caching systems, and cryptographic fingerprinting alike. What's changed most for a tool like this one specifically is where the computation happens: modern JavaScript engines run hash-based Set and Map operations fast enough to deduplicate substantial lists instantly inside a web browser, on data that never leaves the user's device — a capability that would have required a dedicated server-side batch process not many years ago.

invoice-generator.description: Build an itemized invoice with a live preview, multi-currency support, and one-click print/PDF export.

checklist.title: What Makes an Invoice Valid
checklist.intro: Requirements vary by country, but most jurisdictions expect an invoice to include:
items: A unique, sequential invoice number — never reused, even for a cancelled invoice.
The full legal name and address of both the seller and the buyer.
A clear issue date and, separately, a payment due date.
An itemized description of each good or service, not just a lump sum.
The tax rate applied and the tax amount shown separately from the subtotal.
The currency the amounts are stated in, especially for cross-border invoices.

errors.required: Please enter valid tax and discount values.
errors.invalidItem: Each item needs a description, a quantity greater than 0, and a non-negative unit price.
errors.invalidTaxRate: Tax rate must not be negative.

intro.title: How Invoice Totals Actually Add Up
intro.paragraph1: An invoice's math follows a fixed order that matters: every line item's quantity times its unit price is summed into a subtotal, a discount (if any) is subtracted from that subtotal first, and only then is tax calculated — on the discounted amount, not the original subtotal. Applying tax before the discount, or applying it to the pre-discount subtotal, produces a different, incorrect total, which is exactly the kind of ordering mistake this tool's calculation logic is built to never make.
intro.paragraph2: The distinction between an invoice's issue date and its due date is also more than a formality: the gap between them (this tool defaults to 14 days, but 30 is common under the term "Net 30") is the actual interest-free credit period a seller is extending to a buyer, which is why standard payment terms like "Net 30" or "Net 60" are really shorthand for a specific amount of short-term financing built into the transaction.

diagram.caption: The fixed order of invoice math: discount is subtracted from the subtotal first, and tax is calculated on what's left — never on the original subtotal.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: Two worked examples showing the exact order discount and tax are applied in.

rows.scenario: 2 items: 10×$50 design work, 1×$20 hosting, 15% tax, no discount

items.question: Is a discount applied before or after tax?
items.answer: Before — a discount reduces the subtotal first, and tax is then calculated on that already-discounted amount. Applying tax to the original subtotal and then subtracting the discount produces a different (and incorrect) total whenever both a discount and a tax rate are in play, which is why the order genuinely matters.

items.question: What's the difference between an invoice and a receipt?
items.answer: An invoice is a request for payment, issued before money changes hands, and it establishes a debt the buyer owes. A receipt is proof that payment has already been received. The same document can't correctly serve as both at once — a paid invoice is typically followed by a separate receipt, not relabeled as one.

items.question: What does "Net 30" actually mean?
items.answer: It means full payment is due within 30 days of the invoice's issue date — not 30 days after the goods or services were delivered, and not 30 calendar days from an arbitrary date. "Net 15" and "Net 60" follow the same logic with a different day count; the "Net" simply signals no early-payment discount applies to the stated amount.

items.question: Why does every invoice need a unique invoice number?
items.answer: It's the specific reference both the buyer's and seller's accounting systems use to match a payment to the exact invoice it settles, and in most tax jurisdictions, sequential invoice numbering is also a compliance requirement that makes it harder to conceal deleted or backdated invoices during an audit.

items.question: Is this tool's invoice legally compliant for my country?
items.answer: This tool covers the fields most jurisdictions commonly require, but exact legal requirements vary by country — some require a tax registration number, a specific VAT breakdown, or a particular language. Treat this as a strong starting template, not a substitute for checking your local tax authority's specific invoicing rules.

items.question: Why show the currency explicitly instead of assuming everyone uses the same one?
items.answer: Because an invoice with an ambiguous currency is a real, common source of payment disputes in cross-border business — "$500" alone doesn't specify US, Canadian, Australian, or several other dollars, and stating the currency code (USD, EUR, AED) removes that ambiguity entirely.

history.title: 5,000 Years Before the First Spreadsheet
history.paragraph: The invoice is one of the oldest surviving forms of business documentation: archaeologists have recovered clay tablets from the Sumerian city of Uruk, dating to roughly 3400–3300 BCE, recording deliveries of grain, wool, and beer to temple estates — administrative proof that a transaction had actually taken place. These tablets predate even the earliest fully developed writing systems, meaning record-keeping needs are part of what drove writing itself to be invented, not the other way around. The core function hasn't changed in five millennia: a durable, portable record establishing what was owed, by whom, for what.

modernDevelopments.title: From Paper Ledgers to Structured Data
modernDevelopments.paragraph: For most of that history, an invoice was whatever the seller wrote down — free-form, unstructured, and readable only by a human. That changed with electronic invoicing standards like UBL (Universal Business Language), standardized internationally as ISO/IEC 19845, which defines a strict, machine-readable XML structure for an invoice's fields — issuer, buyer, line items, tax breakdown — so accounting software on both ends of a transaction can process it automatically without a human re-typing anything. Government-mandated e-invoicing built on standards like this is now routine across the EU, and in Turkey, Peru, Colombia, and Panama, among others.

glossary.title: Costing Terms Explained
glossary.intro: The vocabulary of inventory costing, in plain language.

rows.meaning: Assumes the oldest purchased units are sold first, so what remains in stock is valued at the most recent purchase prices.
Assumes the most recently purchased units are sold first, so what remains in stock is valued at the oldest purchase prices.

intro.title: How Inventory Costing Actually Works
intro.paragraph1: When a business buys the same product at different prices over time — a common reality as suppliers raise prices or run promotions — it has to decide, on paper, which purchase price to assign to the units it sold and which price to assign to the units still sitting on the shelf. This is not a physical question about which literal box left the warehouse; it is an accounting convention. FIFO assumes the oldest purchase layer is sold first, leaving the newest, usually more expensive, cost basis in ending inventory. LIFO assumes the opposite: the newest layer is sold first, leaving the oldest, usually cheaper, cost basis behind. Weighted-average sidesteps the ordering question entirely by blending every purchase into one cost per unit and applying it uniformly.
intro.paragraph2: The choice is not cosmetic — it changes reported numbers. In a period of rising prices, FIFO assigns the cheaper, older cost to Cost of Goods Sold, which inflates reported profit and the tax bill that follows it, while leaving a higher-value ending inventory on the balance sheet. LIFO does the reverse: it assigns the pricier, newer cost to COGS, shrinking reported profit and tax exposure, while leaving a lower, often stale-looking inventory value on the balance sheet. Weighted-average lands in between, smoothing out the swings of individual purchase lots. None of the three methods is 'more correct' in isolation — they simply answer 'what did this sale cost us?' with three different, equally defensible conventions.

diagram.caption: The same three purchase layers, drawn down in opposite order: FIFO consumes the oldest (bottom) layer first; LIFO consumes the newest (top) layer first.

examples.title: Worked Examples
examples.intro: The same purchase history, valued three different ways.

Buy 10 units @ $5, sell none this period
rows.result: All three methods agree: ending value $50

items.question: Which costing method should my business actually use?
items.answer: It depends on your reporting goals and, in many jurisdictions, on tax rules — under IFRS, LIFO is not permitted at all, while US GAAP permits it. FIFO tends to mirror the physical flow of perishable or fast-moving goods and produces a balance sheet inventory value closer to current replacement cost. LIFO can reduce taxable income during inflationary periods. Weighted-average is often chosen for its simplicity when individual purchase lots are hard to track separately, such as with bulk commodities.

items.question: Why do FIFO, LIFO, and weighted-average give different ending inventory values from the exact same purchases?
items.answer: Because each method makes a different assumption about which purchase price gets assigned to the units that were sold versus the units left in stock. The total units and the total dollars spent purchasing them are identical across all three methods — only how that total is split between Cost of Goods Sold and ending inventory value changes.

items.question: Does the costing method have to match the actual physical order units leave the warehouse?
items.answer: No. FIFO and LIFO are accounting cost-flow assumptions, not requirements about physical handling. A warehouse can physically ship its oldest stock first (a real FIFO picking policy) while its books are kept on LIFO, or vice versa — the accounting convention and the physical logistics are independent decisions.

items.question: Why does weighted-average recompute a single unit cost instead of tracking layers?
items.answer: Because it treats every unit in stock as interchangeable rather than tied to a specific purchase lot. The average cost is simply total cost of all purchases divided by total units purchased — every unit sold or remaining is valued at that same blended rate, which is why weighted-average is the simplest method to compute by hand.

items.question: How does this tool decide which units are 'sold' when I enter a units-sold number?
items.answer: It draws down your purchase batches in the order you entered them (oldest first) for FIFO, in reverse order for LIFO, and applies the single blended average cost for weighted-average — this calculator does not change your batch order for you, so enter batches from oldest purchase to newest for the layer logic to be correct.

items.question: What does the low-stock flag mean, and does it change with the costing method?
items.answer: It compares your ending unit count — the number of units left after the units-sold figure is subtracted — against the reorder threshold you set. The unit count itself is identical across FIFO, LIFO, and weighted-average, since costing method only changes the dollar value assigned to those units, not how many there are.

history.title: A Debate as Old as Modern Accounting
history.paragraph: First-in-first-out and last-in-first-out costing both emerged as formal accounting practices in the United States in the early 20th century, but LIFO's use accelerated sharply after the US Congress formally permitted it for tax purposes in the Revenue Act of 1938 — a period of rising raw material costs where LIFO's lower reported profit meant a lower tax bill. The choice between FIFO and LIFO became one of the most studied topics in accounting research through the mid-20th century, since it directly affects reported earnings, tax liability, and how comparable one company's financial statements are to another's.

modernDevelopments.title: One Global Standard Diverges from the Other
modernDevelopments.paragraph: The clearest modern development is a split rather than a convergence: International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), under IAS 2, prohibit LIFO entirely, while United States Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (US GAAP) continue to permit it. This means a multinational company can be required to report different inventory values for the same physical stock depending on which accounting standard applies, and it is a standing obstacle to full convergence between the two global accounting frameworks. Weighted-average costing, permitted under both standards, has correspondingly grown in popularity as a method that avoids this jurisdictional divide.

intro.title: How Break-Even Analysis Actually Works
intro.paragraph1: Every unit sold contributes a fixed amount — its contribution margin, price minus variable cost — toward covering the business's fixed costs, which don't change no matter how many units are sold. The break-even point is simply the moment those accumulated contributions exactly equal the fixed costs: sell fewer units than that and the business runs at a loss, sell more and every additional unit's contribution margin becomes pure profit, since the fixed costs are already fully covered.
intro.paragraph2: This is exactly why a business with high fixed costs but a high contribution margin per unit (like software, where marginal cost per additional user is near zero) can be unprofitable at low volume and extremely profitable at scale, while a business with low fixed costs but thin per-unit margins breaks even quickly but scales up profit much more slowly. The same math extends past simply breaking even: adding a target profit on top of fixed costs and dividing by the contribution margin answers a more useful real question — not "when do I stop losing money," but "how many units get me to the profit I actually want."

diagram.caption: The classic CVP chart: fixed costs set a flat floor, total cost rises with volume, revenue rises faster — the crossing point is the break-even point, splitting the chart into a loss zone and a profit zone.

items.question: What's the difference between a fixed cost and a variable cost?
items.answer: A fixed cost stays the same regardless of sales volume — rent is rent whether you sell 10 units or 10,000. A variable cost scales directly with each unit sold — the materials in one more product, the commission on one more sale. Break-even analysis treats these two categories completely differently precisely because they behave differently as volume changes.

items.question: Why does the contribution margin matter more than the profit margin here?
items.answer: Because contribution margin (price minus variable cost) tells you exactly how much each additional sale contributes toward covering fixed costs — and once fixed costs are fully covered, every further unit's contribution margin becomes pure profit. Overall profit margin blends fixed and variable costs together, which hides that specific mechanic.

items.question: Can a business ever break even in dollars but not in units, or vice versa?
items.answer: No — break-even units and break-even revenue are two views of the exact same point, since break-even revenue is just break-even units multiplied by the price per unit. They always describe the identical moment where total revenue equals total cost.

items.question: Why round break-even units up instead of to the nearest whole number?
items.answer: Because a fractional unit isn't a real sale — 333.3 units doesn't cover fixed costs, only 334 whole units does. Rounding down would show a break-even point the business hasn't actually reached yet, which defeats the purpose of the calculation.

items.question: Does break-even analysis account for changing prices or costs over time?
items.answer: No — this is a snapshot model that assumes fixed costs, variable cost per unit, and price all stay constant across the full range being analyzed. It's most accurate for a specific planning period at a specific price point, and needs to be recalculated whenever any of those three inputs actually change.

items.question: What does it mean if a break-even calculation returns no valid answer?
items.answer: It means the price per unit doesn't exceed the variable cost per unit — every sale loses money before fixed costs even enter the picture, so no volume of sales, however large, could ever reach break-even. That's a pricing problem, not a volume problem, and no amount of extra sales fixes it.

history.title: From a 1903 Chart to a Depression-Era Standard
history.paragraph: The graphical idea behind break-even analysis dates back further than the term itself: engineer Henry Hess published an early chart plotting cost against volume in 1903, and Charles E. Knoeppel formalized the distinction between fixed and variable costs in 1918. It was Columbia University professor Walter Rautenstrauch who, in his 1930 book The Successful Control of Profits, coined the actual term "break-even point" and popularized the chart as a standard planning tool — timing that mattered enormously, since the Great Depression's collapse in demand forced businesses across the board to understand exactly how far sales could fall before they started losing money.

modernDevelopments.title: From a Hand-Drawn Chart to a Spreadsheet Input
modernDevelopments.paragraph: Break-even analysis is now a standard component of management accounting and startup financial planning, taught as part of cost-volume-profit (CVP) analysis in virtually every accounting curriculum. Its modern extensions include multi-product break-even analysis (blending several products' different contribution margins into one combined break-even point) and sensitivity analysis, which tests how the break-even point shifts if a specific cost or price assumption turns out to be wrong — exactly the kind of instant recalculation this tool's live chart is built to show.
